--- title: '1D diffusion model solution' author: 'Sasha D. Hafner' --- Let's start by looking at the measurement data. We'll use pandas. ::: {#e836710b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd ``` ::: ::: {#b193a4f3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} measdat = pd.read_csv('col_salt.csv') measdat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

We can match that exactly without changing the `diff1D()` function and align model output and measurements without a merge operation. But, for graphical validation, it is usually best to use a high resolution to get a smooth curve. Load our model function. ::: {#296feb53 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import diff_mod as dm ``` ::: And other modules. ::: {#568ac4a0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ``` ::: So here is our model call. We'll use a high resolution (100 points) for a smooth curve. ::: {#b344d3e4 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} pred01 = dm.diff1D( L = 0.1, n = 50, D = 1.6E-9, bc = [36, 0], ci = 0, t_eval = np.linspace(0, 20 * 86400, 100) ) ``` ::: And we can use the same approach that was shown in the exercise for calculating accumulation. We will need the cross-sectional area. ::: {#c5a7c1c8 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} area = np.pi * (0.02 / 2)**2 area ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.0003141592653589793 ``` ::: ::: The `numpy.sum()` function accepts an axis parameter (second parameter). The help file doesn't really illuminate how to set it, but with experimentation you can figure out how to add up all the columns, so you have one sum per time. Mass units in model output are kg, and the measurement data are in mg. So we will convert to mg here. ::: {#6e642dbd .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} salt_mod_mg = (pred01['c'] * 1e6 * pred01['dx'] * area).sum(0) salt_mod_mg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([ 0. , 66.8265291 , 94.94589329, 116.46024663, 134.57851454, 150.53093845, 164.94818074, 178.20238801, 190.53689802, 202.11938285, 213.07188051, 223.48576386, 233.43057884, 242.9617374 , 252.12192994, 260.94656446, 269.46362299, 277.69628009, 285.66451838, 293.38359465, 300.86816662, 308.12947442, 315.178295 , 322.02376961, 328.67345864, 335.13578279, 341.41628933, 347.52211055, 353.45805775, 359.23023022, 364.8434572 , 370.30227857, 375.61176497, 380.77541216, 385.79849037, 390.68411611, 395.43669446, 400.05969297, 404.55641156, 408.93130941, 413.18656273, 417.32638395, 421.35331682, 425.27085313, 429.0819469 , 432.78925412, 436.39603037, 439.90435168, 443.31767626, 446.6378755 , 449.86805732, 453.01034458, 456.06712888, 459.04115301, 461.9339505 , 464.74848782, 467.48624702, 470.1497813 , 472.7407894 , 475.26139178, 477.71361208, 480.0990236 , 482.4197663 , 484.67728138, 486.87357747, 489.0100775 , 491.08856389, 493.11057798, 495.07757383, 496.99120384, 498.85266623, 500.66370608, 502.42542509, 504.13930893, 505.80662168, 507.42854979, 509.006528 , 510.54148657, 512.03481013, 513.48748211, 514.90072211, 516.27554763, 517.61299837, 518.91413871, 520.17984571, 521.41122413, 522.60906109, 523.77440693, 524.90804579, 526.01087698, 527.0837737 , 528.12745271, 529.14283043, 530.13056104, 531.09148218, 532.02625516, 532.93564119, 533.82031598, 534.68092092, 535.51817484]) ``` ::: ::: And time there is in h. Finally, let's plot the results for comparison. ::: {#4d3f19db .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} plt.plot(measdat.time_d, measdat.salt_mg, marker = 'o', label = 'Measured') plt.plot(pred01['t'] / 86400, salt_mod_mg, label = 'Model output') plt.xlabel('Time (d)') plt.ylabel('Column NaCl (mg)') plt.legend() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](validation_solution_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=594 height=431} ::: ::: Well, clearly the model underestimates NaCl accumulation, even if we consider that there is some random error in measurements (see it?). But measurements and the model both show the same shape and are not terribly far off. We can get quantitative using the model fit statistics we discussed in class on Thursday. But we now need to be completly sure that the times in the measurement and model line up. There are a couple ways to do this. If measurement times are regularly spaced (they are here, see above), we could use `np.linspace()` but with the right number of times and spacing. But a more flexible and probably safer approach is to just extract the times from the measurements and put them in the model call like this. ::: {#950c06ee .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} pred02 = dm.diff1D( L=0.1, n=50, D=1.6E-9, bc=[36, 0], ci=0, t_eval = measdat['time_d'] * 86400 ) ``` ::: ::: {#22eab0ef .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} salt_mod2_mg = (pred02['c'] * 1e6 * pred01['dx'] * area).sum(0) salt_mod2_mg ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` array([ 0. , 149.77397805, 212.00223581, 259.64298207, 299.38939487, 333.53749457, 363.17582796, 388.98943544, 411.49866496, 431.13365655, 448.2640516 , 463.21008921, 476.25048539, 487.62803763, 497.55500934, 506.21628765, 513.77330909, 520.36672581, 526.11948628, 531.13881895, 535.51817484]) ``` ::: ::: I created a module with the model fit functions from the book. Let's load it. ::: {#ff338e22 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import mod_fit as mf ``` ::: We were careful with the time alignment, so we could do, e.g, this, for RMSE: ::: {#6a517bcb .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} mf.rmse(measdat['salt_mg'], salt_mod2_mg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` np.float64(45.86101042417123) ``` ::: ::: So the RMSE is about 46 mg. Comparing to the plot, that makes some sense. We can also combine measurements and model output in a single DataFrame. First, make a new data frame that will hold measurements and model output. ::: {#41d953c1 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} mmdat = measdat.copy() ``` ::: And add the model output we processed above. ::: {#fc2cfe92 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} mmdat['salt_mod_mg'] = salt_mod2_mg mmdat ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

First mean bias. ::: {#f96f6d61 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} mf.mbe(mmdat.salt_mg, mmdat.salt_mod_mg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` np.float64(-42.657897805438196) ``` ::: ::: So that's a mean bias of under 10% of the maximum. That would not be terrible for an environmental model, but depending on the application, better accuracy might be needed. Mean absolute error is similar. ::: {#b75fabed .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} mf.mae(mmdat.salt_mg, mmdat.salt_mod_mg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` np.float64(42.657897805438196) ``` ::: ::: Not surprising, from looking at the plot, which shows that most of the error is related to bias.
